cases.note: Read the other way round it is a total loss of enforcement, which is why the contract states it twice.
The low-score rule matches and is not in this endpoint's chain.

**Do not fall back to the whole chain when narrowing empties it.** Rail Center has a fallback of exactly that shape and it belongs to the publishing side alone: it drops a binding whose policies are all absent or disabled before the bundle is written. Copying it here makes the two sides disagree — deny there, allow here.
The same empty narrowing by the other route, and the one a publishing-side fallback would turn into a denial by the whole chain.
Both sides of the membership test are canonicalised, so a non-canonically spelled id matches its policy rather than nothing.
A lower priority number is genuinely higher precedence rather than merely earlier in a list that keeps being read.
Numerically, not as text: a default string comparator gets this backwards.
An implementation reading two equal priorities must not be free to choose, or two readers would answer differently exactly where the policies conflict.
A decision reporting the bundle's own spelling names the same policy two ways across a decision and its denial report.
An implementation reporting the first rule in its chain produces a record that is wrong and that nothing downstream will contradict.
An alert that matched on a request a later denial stopped is still something an operator asked to be told about.
Listed at priorities [2, 3, 1] precisely so a reader that accumulates in bundle order fails it.
A disabled policy is skipped, not evaluated and discarded.
The remedy for a rule nobody can read is to switch it off, and that only works if disabling is decided before interpreting.

**The refusal is lazy.** The walk stops at the first match, so a rule at priority 9 is never reached once priority 1 has denied, and that request has a clean answer. Refusing the whole bundle up front turns one bad condition into a total outage and answers differently here.

What separates 'refuse the request' from 'refuse but keep the alerts' and from 'skip the rule and keep walking'. Alerts already accumulated are discarded with the decision: they were the first half of a verdict that was never reached.
The refusal comes first in the chain, so the walk ends there whatever the later rule would have answered.

policies.name: Deny an agent with no baseline

cases.note: A null score is an absent one. A reader that lets a null read as present stops this rule firing on exactly the agents it exists for — and `lt 40` would not catch them either, since an ordered operator does not hold against an absence.
The other half of the pair above, and why the seeded chain needs both rules rather than one.
The rule the whole file is about. No entry, so the fallback answers and the chain is never reached.
A bundle with bindings is not a bundle where every endpoint is bound. Reading a non-empty `bindings` as 'this bundle narrows, so walk it' refuses nothing here.
An entry exists, so the fallback has nothing to say and the binding narrows as it always does.
`open` is an entry. An endpoint an operator deliberately exempted is not one nobody has reviewed, and the most restrictive posture must not convert the one into the other.
Not refused for being unbound — which is not the same as unjudged. The whole chain still judges it, and may still deny.
The half an implementation gets wrong. `observe` is what an operator uses to be sure nothing is blocked; a fallback consulted here blocks.
There is no endpoint, so a fallback about endpoints has nothing to refuse. Refusing here would let the strictest posture close the messages a session opens with.

It named an endpoint; the reader declined to compose a key for it. No binding can match a key that was never composed, and the input a reader understands least is not the one to give the benefit of the doubt.
The other half: `pass` hands it to the whole chain, which is where the endpoint-derived rules catch it.

The half that stops `pass` being read as `unjudged`. The fallback does not refuse the call and the chain then does, so a reader that forwarded an unbound endpoint without walking it would answer `refused: false` correctly here and still admit the request the chain denies.

The other half, and why the one above is not simply `block` by another name. Same bundle, same endpoint, same absence of a binding — only the ticket differs, so the verdict is the chain's and not the fallback's.
The same request the case above allows. `block` refuses it without consulting the chain, which is what makes 'the chain is not consulted' observable: consult it and this call is allowed.
